_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
part of https://devicechain.io/releases.json (see hack/build-release-manifest.sh).
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING — and update `version`,
`theme`, `breaking` and `highlights` TOGETHER. They are one record of one release, and
the way this file goes wrong is three of the four moving while the fourth keeps last
release's answer: a theme naming work that is not in the highlights below it reads as
confidently as one that is. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
`theme` IS THE ONE PHRASE THAT NAMES THE RELEASE — a chapter title, not a changelog
line. It leads the GitHub release notes and it reaches releases.json, so it is the
first thing a reader decides against. A good one names what changed about the system:
"the instance is declared, not remembered". A bad one is a category ("bug fixes and
improvements"), the version restated, or the first highlight with its verbs filed off —
if it would fit any release, it is not this release's theme.
Write a PHRASE. The guard caps it at 72 characters, the width of a commit subject,
because past that you are writing a sentence, and a sentence about what changed is a
highlight — there is already a list for those below. The cap is the only taste this
file can enforce; the rest is on you.
🔴 The theme is PUBLISHED, and so is every highlight — into the GitHub release body and
into devicechain.io/releases.json. No ADR references in either: ADRs live in a repo the
reader cannot open, so a citation is a dead reference dressed as a source. Say the thing
itself, or link to a public page. THIS BLOCK IS DIFFERENT — `_comment` is published
nowhere, it is the only part of the file a reader never sees, and it may cite ADR-080 or
any other freely. The guard reads exactly that distinction: it scans `theme` and
`highlights[]`, case-insensitively, and leaves this block alone.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in the website's download menu, not in a
document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` MEANS 'THIS RELEASE HAS BREAKING CHANGES'. It does NOT mean 'you must recreate
your instance', and this comment used to say it did — it told you to set the flag when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`. The website has not read it that way since the
copy was repaired: `true` renders exactly one sentence, 'This release has breaking changes
— read the release notes before upgrading', and `false` renders nothing at all. So set it
true whenever something breaks for SOMEBODY — an API caller, an operator, a package
consumer — and use the first highlight to say who, and whether the upgrade itself is
ordinary. If a release ever genuinely requires recreating an instance, give that its OWN
manifest field rather than overloading this one a second time.
The other correction: there is no docs banner. Nothing under docs/ fetches releases.json.
The website download menu is this file's only consumer.
For each highlight, ask whether it makes a sentence on the marketing site stale. The
site is a separate repository and nothing here reads its prose. Answering "no site
impact" is a fine answer; not asking is not.
theme: sized from measurement at 6,000 events a second; a full stream refuses
highlights: Count your event store before you upgrade. The upgrade from v0.18.0 (`dcctl install`, then `dcctl upgrade`) rebuilds the event store's keys over every row not yet compressed, and an instance with more than 4,000,000 such rows cannot be upgraded in place: export what you need, then recreate it. Count before running this release's `dcctl install`: destroying with `--keep-backups` keeps only the instance's event history, and the upgrade guide says what that does and does not bring back. That is about a week at 2 events a second, each with one reading and one anchor, so most instances with real traffic are over the line. An event table with more than 500 chunks is refused as well, until its oldest chunks are removed, which deletes every tenant's events in them for good. `dcctl upgrade` now also applies the instance's message broker and event store settings, so it must run where the instance was bootstrapped, and it restarts both. Each node running a NATS server needs room for its larger request first: 500m CPU and 768Mi memory, less with `--compact`. Without `--compact`, the services that handle every event also need several more CPU cores free while they roll. Also before upgrading: a tenant's ingest ceiling now counts readings rather than messages, an event carries at most 256 readings, a reading dated more than 366 days before it arrives is refused, `backup_retention` is split into one setting per database, a `device-state` or `event-management` pool of 10 connections or fewer needs its writer count (`projection.writers`, `persistence.writers`) set, and on an `--ha` install without `--compact` analytics readers may hold at most 17 event-store connections in total. An MQTT source reading a broker you run now connects as `devicechain:<instance>:<source>:<pod>`, so a broker rule naming the client id `devicechain` must allow that prefix, a broker must accept an id longer than 23 characters, and messages it receives while the upgrade rolls can be stored twice unless you pause the publishers on your broker. The upgrade guide lists every step.

A default HA install keeps pace at 6,000 events a second. On a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster of three 4-vCPU, 16 GB database nodes and three 4-vCPU, 8 GB service nodes, it accepted 6,000 events a second for 10 minutes, twice, and stored every accepted event exactly once, checked event by event with none missing, none stored twice and none unexpected; every stage kept pace and the backlog drained within 3 seconds. Each event carried one reading, from one tenant whose ingest ceiling was raised for the test, so that is above the 5,000 readings a second one tenant's devices can be admitted at the default ingest ceiling. The event-path services now request the CPU they use at that rate and prefer different nodes, and the event store updates fewer indexes and writes less write-ahead log for each event.

A full ingest stream now refuses new events before it would discard unread ones, apart from the few cases the upgrade guide names. When a consumer's unread backlog nears its stream's capacity, or the already-processed events a full stream still holds are about to run out, HTTP ingest answers `503` with `Retry-After` for every tenant, since the streams are shared, MQTT messages wait at the broker, and Sparkplug, LwM2M and external-broker readings are dropped and counted. Two new alerts report a backlog nearing the line and the refusal itself. Over HTTP, a tenant over its own ingest ceiling is answered `429` before that check is made.

Backups are kept longer, and the archived log is smaller. The relational database can be recovered to any point in the last 30 days, the event store the last 7, so a deleted tenant's core data also stays restorable from backups for 30 days rather than 7. The archived log is compressed with zstd, base backups can be volume snapshots (`--backup-snapshot-class`), and the in-cluster backup store is sized so the event store fills first. `dcctl destroy` now deletes an instance's in-cluster backups unless you pass `--keep-backups`.

Databases can be placed on nodes you choose (`--database-node-selector`, `--database-toleration`), and their primaries prefer different nodes. A new OpenTofu configuration creates a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster with separate database and service pools. Running `dcctl bootstrap` again now finishes an instance whose first bootstrap failed late, while installing the chart or waiting for the services to become ready; upgrade every copy of `dcctl` you use before running it against an instance this release built. Any service can serve Go runtime profiles on an opt-in loopback listener. A revoked device credential can now take up to five seconds to stop working on a replica that missed the change.
